en.g: a duchess; the wife or widow of a duke

23410.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse hertoginna (“duchess”), corresponding to hertogi (“duke”) with the feminine suffix -inna (“feminine noun suffix”). The base hertogi was likely borrowed from Middle Low German hertôge (“duke”), from Old Saxon heritogo (“army leader”), ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *harjatogō (“army leader, commander”), literally “army leader”.
By surface analysis, hertug (“duke”) + -inne (“feminine noun suffix”).
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk hertuginne, Danish hertuginde, Swedish hertiginna, Dutch hertogin and German Herzogin (“duchess”). Compare also the parallel formation Icelandic

24434.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse *hyldr (“hulder”), genitive huldar, from Old Norse hylja (“to hide, cover”), from Proto-Germanic *huljaną (“to cover, veil”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- (“to hide”). Compare Old Norse Huld, the name of a sorceress or giantess. The underlying sense is thus “the hidden one” or “the concealed one”.
The word is etymologically unrelated to hul (“hollow”); the traditional hollow-back motif belongs to the folklore and is not the source of the name.
Compare cognates of the underlying verb: Icelandic hylja, Faroese hylja, Swedish hölja, Danish hylle, Dutch hullen

Internationalism, from the international name of the city of Djibouti; the country was named after its capital. Compare French Djibouti, used during the former French administration and retained as one of the country's official-language names.

Parallel international adaptations include Danish Djibouti, Swedish Djibouti, German Dschibuti, Polish Dżibuti, Spanish Yibuti and English Djibouti

1004658.etyen:
From bonde (“farmer, peasant”) + pike (“girl, young woman”). The first element, bonde, continues Old Norse bóndi (“farmer, householder”), originally the present participle of a verb meaning “to dwell, live”. The second element, pike, continues Old Norse píka (“young girl”), possibly through Old Swedish pika from Finnish piika (“maid, servant girl”); its ultimate origin is uncertain.
Compare Danish bondepige and Swedish bondflicka (“farm girl, peasant girl”).

1004914.etyen:
From fag (“field, profession”) + samling (“gathering, meeting”), literally “professional-field gathering”.
The first element, fag (“field, subject, profession”), is borrowed from Low German fak (“compartment, field”), originally referring to something delimited or joined together and later developing the senses “field, discipline, profession”. The second element, samling (“gathering, meeting”), is a verbal noun derived from samle (“to gather, collect”) + -ing. samle is probably from Middle Low German samelen (“to gather, collect”); compare Old Norse samna (“to gather”).
